items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The model of membrane structure in which proteins are embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer and can move laterally"?
items.answer: fluid mosaic model
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of fluid mosaic model.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Davson–Danielli model and the fluid mosaic model.
items.answer: Davson–Danielli proposed a static bilayer sandwiched between continuous protein layers; the fluid mosaic model has proteins embedded in or attached to a fluid bilayer, able to move laterally.
items.markingKey: Davson–Danielli proposed a static bilayer sandwiched between continuous protein layers; the fluid mosaic model has proteins embedded in or attached to a fluid bilayer, able to move laterally. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the properties of phospholipids lead to the formation of a bilayer.
items.answer: Phospholipids are amphipathic; in water the hydrophilic heads associate with water and the hydrophobic tails are excluded and face each other, forming two layers; this arrangement is energetically stable and self-sealing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Phospholipids are amphipathic; in water the hydrophilic heads associate with water and the hydrophobic tails are excluded and face each other, forming two layers; this arrangement is energetically stable and self-sealing. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Draw and label a diagram of the fluid mosaic model. List the components that should be shown.
items.answer: Phospholipid bilayer (heads and tails labelled), integral (transmembrane) protein, peripheral protein, channel protein, glycoprotein with carbohydrate facing outward, cholesterol between phospholipids, inner/outer surfaces labelled.
items.markingKey: Phospholipid bilayer (heads and tails labelled), integral (transmembrane) protein, peripheral protein, channel protein, glycoprotein with carbohydrate facing outward, cholesterol between phospholipids, inner/outer surfaces labelled.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "In the fluid mosaic model, proteins form a continuous layer over the bilayer." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: That was the Davson–Danielli model; in the fluid mosaic model proteins are scattered like a mosaic within and on the fluid bilayer.
items.markingKey: That was the Davson–Danielli model; in the fluid mosaic model proteins are scattered like a mosaic within and on the fluid bilayer. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Frye–Edidin cell fusion experiment (1970), explain how it illustrates the fluidity of membranes.
items.answer: Mouse and human cells with differently labelled membrane proteins were fused; within 40 minutes the labels were intermixed. Proteins diffuse laterally in the bilayer, supporting the fluid nature of the model.
items.markingKey: Context (Mouse and human cells with differently labelled membrane proteins were fused; within 40 minutes the labels were intermixed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Proteins diffuse laterally in the bilayer, supporting the fluid nature of the model. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the fluidity of membranes.

items.stem:
Beetroot discs of equal size were washed, then placed in water at different temperatures for 15 minutes. The absorbance of the water (a measure of red betalain pigment leaking from the vacuoles) was measured with a colorimeter. Three discs were used at each temperature.

Temperature / °C | Absorbance 1 | Absorbance 2 | Absorbance 3
20 | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.05
30 | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.05

50 | 0.37 | 0.36 | 0.40
60 | 0.74 | 0.87 | 0.72

80 | 0.96 | 1.04 | 0.91

(a) Calculate the mean absorbance at 40 °C. [1]
(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the absorbance readings at 40 °C. [1]
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in mean absorbance between 30 °C and 80 °C. [2]

Cylinders of sweet potato were weighed, placed in sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 24 hours at 25 °C, blotted and reweighed.

Sucrose / mol dm⁻³ | Initial mass / g | Final mass / g | % change in mass
0.0 | 2.06 | 2.41 | +17.0
0.1 | 1.85 | 2.06 | +11.4
0.2 | 2.30 | 2.40 | +4.3
0.3 | 2.28 | 2.24 | ?
0.4 | 2.14 | 1.95 | -8.9
0.5 | 1.94 | 1.61 | -17.0

(a) Calculate the percentage change in mass in 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. [2]
(b) Explain why the results were expressed as percentage change in mass rather than change in mass. [1]
(c) Estimate the sucrose concentration that is isotonic with the tissue. [2]
(d) Explain the change in mass in 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. [2]
items.answer: (a) -1.8 % (b) The cylinders had different initial masses; percentage change allows fair comparison. (c) ≈ 0.27 mol dm⁻³ (d) The solution is hypertonic to the cells (lower water potential); water leaves the cells by osmosis through the partially permeable membranes, so mass decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (2.24 − 2.28)/2.28 × 100 (M1) = -1.8 % (A1). (b) [1] Different starting masses (A1). (c) [2] Concentration where % change = 0, by interpolation between the bracketing values (M1); ≈ 0.27 mol dm⁻³ (A1). (d) [2] Hypertonic / lower water potential outside (A1); water leaves by osmosis (A1).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "fluid mosaic model".
items.answer: The model of membrane structure in which proteins are embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer and can move laterally
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the model of membrane structure in which proteins are embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer and can move laterally. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: What did the fusion of mouse and human cells (Frye and Edidin, 1970) show?
options: Proteins are on the surface only.
Membrane proteins can move laterally within the bilayer.
items.answer: Membrane proteins can move laterally within the bilayer.
items.markingKey: C. Labelled proteins mixed within 40 minutes.

items.stem: Why are integral proteins amphipathic?
options: Their hydrophobic regions lie within the bilayer core and hydrophilic regions face the aqueous surroundings.
items.answer: Their hydrophobic regions lie within the bilayer core and hydrophilic regions face the aqueous surroundings.
items.markingKey: C. Matching the environment of each region.

items.stem: In a TEM image at × 2 000 000, a plasma membrane appears as two dark lines 16 mm apart from outer edge to outer edge. What is the membrane thickness?
items.answer: 8 nm

Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The fluid mosaic model is a complete description of membrane structure."
items.answer: It remains the best general model, but modern evidence refines it with domains and restrictions on movement – models are simplifications that are improved over time.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it accounts for the bilayer, embedded proteins and lateral movement, and has survived many tests; it explains selective permeability and membrane flexibility. Arguments against: membranes contain lipid rafts and protein domains that are less fluid than the model implies; cytoskeletal attachments restrict movement of many proteins. Supported judgement: It remains the best general model, but modern evidence refines it with domains and restrictions on movement – models are simplifications that are improved over time.

items.stem: Which protein allows rapid osmosis in kidney collecting duct cells?
items.answer: aquaporin
items.markingKey: C. Aquaporins are water channels.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Diffusion stops when the concentrations are equal because particles stop moving." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Particles keep moving randomly; at equilibrium there is no net movement because movement is equal in both directions.
items.markingKey: Particles keep moving randomly; at equilibrium there is no net movement because movement is equal in both directions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between hypertonic solutions and hypotonic solutions.
items.answer: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell, so water enters; a hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration, so water leaves.
items.markingKey: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell, so water enters; a hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration, so water leaves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A beetroot cylinder had a mass of 2.40 g before and 2.62 g after 30 minutes in a sucrose solution. Calculate the percentage change.
items.markingKey: (final − initial)/initial × 100 = (2.62 − 2.40)/2.40 × 100 (M1) = +9.2 % (A1); sign/direction required.

items.stem: Red blood cells were placed in solutions of different NaCl concentrations. In which would they burst (haemolyse)?
items.answer: distilled water
items.markingKey: A. 0.9 % is isotonic; water is hypotonic.

items.stem: Briefly describe aquaporins in the collecting ducts of the kidney and explain what it reveals about facilitated diffusion of water.
items.answer: ADH causes vesicles containing aquaporins to fuse with membranes, increasing water reabsorption. More channels increase membrane permeability to water, so more water moves out of the filtrate by osmosis.
items.markingKey: Context (ADH causes vesicles containing aquaporins to fuse with membranes, increasing water reabsorption.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: More channels increase membrane permeability to water, so more water moves out of the filtrate by osmosis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to facilitated diffusion of water.

items.stem: Explain the mechanisms of simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis, and outline factors affecting their rates.
items.answer: Simple: through bilayer, non-polar, small; facilitated: channels (ions, gated) and carriers (glucose), specific, saturable; osmosis: water, partially permeable membrane, aquaporins, from low to high solute; factors: gradient, SA, distance/thickness, temperature, number of channel proteins.
items.markingKey: Simple: through bilayer, non-polar, small; facilitated: channels (ions, gated) and carriers (glucose), specific, saturable; osmosis: water, partially permeable membrane, aquaporins, from low to high solute; factors: gradient, SA, distance/thickness, temperature, number of channel proteins.

items.stem: "Osmosis is just a special case of diffusion." Discuss.
items.answer: Osmosis is a form of passive diffusion of water, but it is distinct because it depends on a partially permeable membrane and solute effects on water potential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: water moves down its own concentration (water potential) gradient passively; the same factors (gradient, area, temperature) affect both. Arguments against: osmosis specifically requires a partially permeable membrane that restricts solute movement; much water passes through aquaporins (facilitated) and its movement is driven by solute effects on water potential. Supported judgement: Osmosis is a form of passive diffusion of water, but it is distinct because it depends on a partially permeable membrane and solute effects on water potential. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "osmosis"?
options: The model of membrane structure in which proteins are embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer and can move laterally
The net passive movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration
Describes a solution with the same solute concentration (osmolarity) as the cell, so there is no net movement of water
The ease with which phospholipids and proteins move within a membrane, affected by temperature, fatty acid saturation and cholesterol
items.answer: The net passive movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration
items.markingKey: B. "osmosis" is the net passive movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration.

items.stem: Why can glucose not cross the bilayer by simple diffusion at a useful rate?
options: It is a relatively large polar molecule.
items.answer: It is a relatively large polar molecule.
items.markingKey: B. GLUT carriers are needed.

items.stem: Explain why plant cells do not burst when placed in distilled water.
items.answer: Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells, but the strong cellulose cell wall exerts pressure that resists further expansion; the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells, but the strong cellulose cell wall exerts pressure that resists further expansion; the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Facilitated diffusion uses ATP because proteins are involved." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Facilitated diffusion is passive and uses no ATP; it is active transport that uses ATP.
items.markingKey: Facilitated diffusion is passive and uses no ATP; it is active transport that uses ATP. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The volume of a red blood cell changed from 92 µm³ to 72 µm³ when it was placed in a salt solution. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: -21.7 %; water moves by osmosis into the cell if the solution is hypotonic and out of it if hypertonic.
items.markingKey: % change = (72 − 92)/92 × 100 (M1) = -21.7 % (A1). Explanation (R1): water moves by osmosis into the cell if the solution is hypotonic and out of it if hypertonic.

items.stem: Which process releases digestive enzymes from pancreatic cells?
items.answer: exocytosis
items.markingKey: exocytosis. Secretory vesicles fuse with the membrane.

items.stem: "Endocytosis does not require energy because the membrane is fluid." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Endocytosis and exocytosis require ATP to reshape the membrane and move vesicles, though they depend on membrane fluidity.
items.markingKey: Endocytosis and exocytosis require ATP to reshape the membrane and move vesicles, though they depend on membrane fluidity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: How does the sodium–potassium pump create a membrane potential?
options: It moves more positive charge out (3 Na⁺) than in (2 K⁺).
It moves equal numbers of ions each way.
items.answer: It moves more positive charge out (3 Na⁺) than in (2 K⁺).
items.markingKey: A. Net export of one positive charge per cycle.

items.stem: Briefly describe insulin secretion by β cells of the pancreas and explain what it reveals about exocytosis.
items.answer: Insulin is packaged in vesicles by the Golgi apparatus and released by exocytosis when blood glucose rises. Vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane releases the protein outside the cell without it crossing the bilayer.
items.markingKey: Context (Insulin is packaged in vesicles by the Golgi apparatus and released by exocytosis when blood glucose rises.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane releases the protein outside the cell without it crossing the bilayer. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to exocytosis.

items.stem: A neurone has 1.2 × 10⁶ sodium–potassium pumps each completing 100 cycles per second. How many K⁺ ions enter per second?
Compare active transport with passive transport and explain the role of the sodium–potassium pump in animal cells.
items.answer: Active: against gradient, ATP, pump proteins, specific; passive: down gradient, no ATP, diffusion/facilitated/osmosis. Na/K pump: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP, phosphorylation and conformational change; maintains resting potential, controls cell volume, drives secondary active transport (e.g. Na–glucose cotransport).
items.markingKey: Active: against gradient, ATP, pump proteins, specific; passive: down gradient, no ATP, diffusion/facilitated/osmosis. items.stem: Which organelle produces most of the ATP used for active transport in root hair cells?
items.answer: mitochondrion
items.markingKey: A. Aerobic respiration supplies ATP.

items.stem: Explain how endocytosis and exocytosis depend on the fluidity of membranes.
items.answer: Phospholipids move freely so the membrane can bend; in endocytosis it folds inward and pinches off to form a vesicle; in exocytosis a vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and becomes part of it; both require energy (ATP).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Phospholipids move freely so the membrane can bend; in endocytosis it folds inward and pinches off to form a vesicle; in exocytosis a vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and becomes part of it; both require energy (ATP). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between active transport and passive transport.
items.answer: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using ATP and pump proteins; passive transport (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis) moves substances down a gradient without ATP.
items.markingKey: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using ATP and pump proteins; passive transport (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis) moves substances down a gradient without ATP. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A mammalian neurone has 5.00 × 10⁵ sodium–potassium pumps, each completing 80 cycles per second. In 60 s calculate the number of Na⁺ ions pumped out, the number of K⁺ ions pumped in and the number of ATP molecules used.
items.markingKey: Cycles = 5.00 × 10⁵ × 80 × 60 = 2.40 × 10⁹ (M1); 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, 1 ATP per cycle (A1 A1).

items.stem: "Active transport is the most important membrane transport mechanism in cells." Discuss.
items.answer: Active transport is essential for establishing gradients, but cells depend on a combination of passive and active processes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it creates the ion gradients needed for nerve impulses, secondary transport and osmotic control; it allows uptake of mineral ions against gradients. Arguments against: most gas exchange and water movement depend on passive processes; active transport uses a large share of cell energy, so passive mechanisms are more economical. Supported judgement: Active transport is essential for establishing gradients, but cells depend on a combination of passive and active processes. items.stem: Membranes of cold-water fish contain a higher proportion of which fatty acids?
items.answer: unsaturated fatty acids
items.markingKey: B. Kinks maintain fluidity in the cold.

items.stem: Why do gated channels allow cells to control ion movement?
options: They use ATP to move ions.
They open only in response to a specific signal (voltage or ligand), so movement can be switched on and off.
items.answer: They open only in response to a specific signal (voltage or ligand), so movement can be switched on and off.
items.markingKey: D. Gating gives control.

items.stem: "Cholesterol always makes membranes more rigid." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it reduces fluidity at higher temperatures but prevents excessive rigidity at low temperatures.
items.markingKey: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it reduces fluidity at higher temperatures but prevents excessive rigidity at low temperatures. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Beetroot discs were heated at different temperatures and the red pigment leaking into water was measured. Above 50 °C leakage rose sharply. What is the best explanation?
options: Membranes become more fluid and proteins denature, so membranes lose their barrier function.
The pigment is actively pumped out.
Pigment is made at high temperatures.
items.answer: Membranes become more fluid and proteins denature, so membranes lose their barrier function.
items.markingKey: A. Classic membrane permeability experiment.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Antarctic icefish living at −1.9 °C shows adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity.
items.answer: Their membranes contain a high proportion of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Kinked unsaturated chains prevent membranes becoming rigid at freezing temperatures.
items.markingKey: Context (Their membranes contain a high proportion of polyunsaturated fatty acids.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Kinked unsaturated chains prevent membranes becoming rigid at freezing temperatures. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity.

items.stem: Explain how membrane fluidity is controlled and why gated ion channels are important.
items.answer: Fluidity: temperature; saturated vs unsaturated fatty acids (kinks); cholesterol buffers; homeoviscous adaptation. Importance: endocytosis, protein movement, function of membrane proteins. Gated channels: voltage-gated Na⁺/K⁺ in action potentials; ligand-gated (acetylcholine) at synapses; passive, specific, controlled opening.

items.stem: Define the term "homeoviscous adaptation".
items.answer: Changes in membrane lipid composition, such as more unsaturated fatty acids in the cold, that maintain membrane fluidity
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: changes in membrane lipid composition, such as more unsaturated fatty acids in the cold, that maintain membrane fluidity. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the role of cholesterol in animal cell membranes.
items.answer: Cholesterol fits between phospholipids; at body temperature its rigid rings restrict tail movement, reducing fluidity and permeability to small polar molecules and ions; at low temperatures it prevents tails packing tightly, so fluidity is maintained – it buffers fluidity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Cholesterol fits between phospholipids; at body temperature its rigid rings restrict tail movement, reducing fluidity and permeability to small polar molecules and ions; at low temperatures it prevents tails packing tightly, so fluidity is maintained – it buffers fluidity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it reduces fluidity at higher temperatures but prevents excessive rigidity at low temperatures.
items.markingKey: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it reduces fluidity at higher temperatures but prevents excessive rigidity at low temperatures. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction shows ligand-gated ion channels.
items.answer: Binding of two acetylcholine molecules opens a central pore allowing Na⁺ to flow into the muscle fibre. A specific ligand changes the protein’s shape, opening the channel and depolarising the membrane.
items.markingKey: Context (Binding of two acetylcholine molecules opens a central pore allowing Na⁺ to flow into the muscle fibre.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A specific ligand changes the protein’s shape, opening the channel and depolarising the membrane. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to ligand-gated ion channels.

items.stem: "Cholesterol is harmful and should be removed from the diet completely." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Cholesterol is essential; the concern is excessive LDL levels, so diet should limit, not eliminate, it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: high blood LDL cholesterol is linked to atherosclerosis and heart disease; reducing saturated fat and cholesterol intake lowers risk for many people. Arguments against: cholesterol is an essential membrane component and precursor of steroid hormones and vitamin D; the liver synthesises most of the body’s cholesterol regardless of diet. Supported judgement: Cholesterol is essential; the concern is excessive LDL levels, so diet should limit, not eliminate, it. the fact that membranes are thin

The movement of particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP and specific pump proteins
An earlier model in which the phospholipid bilayer was sandwiched between two continuous layers of protein, later falsified

items.stem: Distinguish between voltage-gated channels and ligand-gated channels.
items.answer: Voltage-gated channels open in response to a change in membrane potential; ligand-gated channels open when a specific signal molecule binds.
items.markingKey: Voltage-gated channels open in response to a change in membrane potential; ligand-gated channels open when a specific signal molecule binds. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Davson–Danielli proposed a static bilayer sandwiched between continuous protein layers; the fluid mosaic model has proteins embedded in or attached to a fluid bilayer, able to move laterally.
items.markingKey: Davson–Danielli proposed a static bilayer sandwiched between continuous protein layers; the fluid mosaic model has proteins embedded in or attached to a fluid bilayer, able to move laterally. items.stem: Distinguish between facilitated diffusion and simple diffusion.
items.answer: Both are passive and move substances down a concentration gradient; simple diffusion occurs directly through the bilayer (small non-polar molecules); facilitated diffusion uses specific channel or carrier proteins (ions, polar molecules) and can saturate.

items.stem: Explain how the sodium–potassium pump works.
items.answer: Three Na⁺ bind from inside; ATP is hydrolysed and the pump is phosphorylated; it changes shape, releasing Na⁺ outside; two K⁺ bind from outside; the phosphate is released and the pump returns to its original shape, releasing K⁺ inside.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Three Na⁺ bind from inside; ATP is hydrolysed and the pump is phosphorylated; it changes shape, releasing Na⁺ outside; two K⁺ bind from outside; the phosphate is released and the pump returns to its original shape, releasing K⁺ inside. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between ligand-gated channels and voltage-gated channels.
items.answer: Voltage-gated channels open in response to a change in membrane potential; ligand-gated channels open when a specific signal molecule binds.
items.markingKey: Voltage-gated channels open in response to a change in membrane potential; ligand-gated channels open when a specific signal molecule binds. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the evidence that led to the replacement of the Davson–Danielli model by the fluid mosaic model.
items.answer: Freeze-fracture EM showed proteins embedded in the bilayer; membrane proteins were found to be varied and amphipathic, so could not form continuous layers; fluorescent labelling of cell fusion showed proteins move; so the model was falsified and replaced.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Freeze-fracture EM showed proteins embedded in the bilayer; membrane proteins were found to be varied and amphipathic, so could not form continuous layers; fluorescent labelling of cell fusion showed proteins move; so the model was falsified and replaced. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Potato cylinders gained mass in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ sucrose and lost mass in 0.4 mol dm⁻³. What can be concluded?
options: The cells are isotonic with 0.4 mol dm⁻³.
The cells are isotonic with 0.1 mol dm⁻³.
The potato cells’ solute concentration is between 0.1 and 0.4 mol dm⁻³.
items.answer: The potato cells’ solute concentration is between 0.1 and 0.4 mol dm⁻³.
items.markingKey: C. Isotonic point lies between gain and loss.

items.stem: A red blood cell has 4.00 × 10⁶ sodium–potassium pumps, each completing 100 cycles per second. In 10 s calculate the number of Na⁺ ions pumped out, the number of K⁺ ions pumped in and the number of ATP molecules used.
items.markingKey: Cycles = 4.00 × 10⁶ × 100 × 10 = 4.00 × 10⁹ (M1); 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, 1 ATP per cycle (A1 A1).

items.stem: With reference to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, explain how it illustrates ligand-gated ion channels.
items.answer: Binding of two acetylcholine molecules opens a central pore allowing Na⁺ to flow into the muscle fibre. A specific ligand changes the protein’s shape, opening the channel and depolarising the membrane.
items.markingKey: Context (Binding of two acetylcholine molecules opens a central pore allowing Na⁺ to flow into the muscle fibre.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A specific ligand changes the protein’s shape, opening the channel and depolarising the membrane. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to ligand-gated ion channels.

items.stem: A membrane protein extracted from cells has a central stretch of 20 non-polar amino acids flanked by charged ones. What is its most likely position?
options: spanning the membrane, with the non-polar stretch in the hydrophobic core
attached only to the outer surface
items.answer: spanning the membrane, with the non-polar stretch in the hydrophobic core
items.markingKey: A. About 20 non-polar residues form one transmembrane helix.

items.stem: Outline one way in which aquaporins in the collecting ducts of the kidney shows facilitated diffusion of water.
items.answer: ADH causes vesicles containing aquaporins to fuse with membranes, increasing water reabsorption. More channels increase membrane permeability to water, so more water moves out of the filtrate by osmosis.
items.markingKey: Context (ADH causes vesicles containing aquaporins to fuse with membranes, increasing water reabsorption.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: More channels increase membrane permeability to water, so more water moves out of the filtrate by osmosis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to facilitated diffusion of water.

items.stem: A student claims: "Endocytosis does not require energy because the membrane is fluid." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Endocytosis and exocytosis require ATP to reshape the membrane and move vesicles, though they depend on membrane fluidity.
items.markingKey: Endocytosis and exocytosis require ATP to reshape the membrane and move vesicles, though they depend on membrane fluidity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Bacteria grown at 10 °C have more unsaturated membrane fatty acids than those grown at 37 °C. What is the most likely reason?
options: to make the membrane rigid in the cold
to keep the membrane fluid at low temperature
items.answer: to keep the membrane fluid at low temperature
items.markingKey: D. Homeoviscous adaptation.

items.stem: Describe the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure and evaluate the evidence for it.
items.answer: Bilayer of amphipathic phospholipids; integral and peripheral proteins; glycoproteins, glycolipids, cholesterol; fluidity, lateral movement. Evidence: freeze-fracture, Frye–Edidin, amphipathic proteins, TEM trilaminar appearance. Falsified Davson–Danielli. Limitations: rafts, cytoskeleton.
items.markingKey: Bilayer of amphipathic phospholipids; integral and peripheral proteins; glycoproteins, glycolipids, cholesterol; fluidity, lateral movement. Evidence: freeze-fracture, Frye–Edidin, amphipathic proteins, TEM trilaminar appearance. Falsified Davson–Danielli. Limitations: rafts, cytoskeleton.

items.stem: "Osmosis is just a special case of diffusion." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Osmosis is a form of passive diffusion of water, but it is distinct because it depends on a partially permeable membrane and solute effects on water potential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: water moves down its own concentration (water potential) gradient passively; the same factors (gradient, area, temperature) affect both. Arguments against: osmosis specifically requires a partially permeable membrane that restricts solute movement; much water passes through aquaporins (facilitated) and its movement is driven by solute effects on water potential. Supported judgement: Osmosis is a form of passive diffusion of water, but it is distinct because it depends on a partially permeable membrane and solute effects on water potential. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Active transport is the most important membrane transport mechanism in cells." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Active transport is essential for establishing gradients, but cells depend on a combination of passive and active processes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it creates the ion gradients needed for nerve impulses, secondary transport and osmotic control; it allows uptake of mineral ions against gradients. Arguments against: most gas exchange and water movement depend on passive processes; active transport uses a large share of cell energy, so passive mechanisms are more economical. Supported judgement: Active transport is essential for establishing gradients, but cells depend on a combination of passive and active processes. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem:
Beetroot discs of equal size were washed, then placed in water at different temperatures for 15 minutes. The absorbance of the water (a measure of red betalain pigment leaking from the vacuoles) was measured with a colorimeter. Three discs were used at each temperature.

Temperature / °C | Absorbance 1 | Absorbance 2 | Absorbance 3
20 | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.05
30 | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.05
40 | 0.09 | 0.08 | 0.08
50 | 0.37 | 0.32 | 0.36
60 | 0.77 | 0.81 | 0.88
70 | 0.83 | 0.91 | 0.97
80 | 0.97 | 0.91 | 0.94

(a) Calculate the mean absorbance at 70 °C. [1]
(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the absorbance readings at 70 °C. [1]
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in mean absorbance between 30 °C and 80 °C. [2]
(d) Describe the trend shown by the data. [2]
(e) Explain the sharp increase in pigment leakage at higher temperatures. [3]
(f) Explain why the discs were washed before the experiment. [1]
(g) Suggest how the experiment could be modified to investigate the effect of ethanol on membranes. [2]
items.answer: (a) 0.90 (b) 0.070 (c) 1780 % (d) Little pigment leaks below about 40 °C; absorbance increases sharply between about 40 and 60 °C, then levels off. (e) Phospholipids gain kinetic energy and the bilayer becomes more fluid/disordered; membrane proteins denature, leaving gaps; the tonoplast and plasma membrane become permeable and pigment leaks out. (f) To remove pigment released from cells cut during preparation, so only leakage during the experiment is measured. (g) Use a range of ethanol concentrations at a constant temperature; same disc size, time and volume; measure absorbance.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (0.83 + 0.91 + 0.97)/3 = 0.90 (A1). (b) [1] SD (n − 1) = 0.070 (A1); accept population SD. (c) [2] Means 0.05 and 0.94 (M1); (0.94 − 0.05)/0.05 × 100 = 1780 % (A1). (d) [2] Low at low temperatures (A1); steep rise at a stated range (A1). (e) [3] Increased fluidity (A1); protein denaturation (A1); membranes lose barrier function (A1). (f) [1] Remove pigment from cut cells (A1). (g) [2] IV ethanol concentration with temperature controlled (A1); same DV method (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fluid mosaic model"?
options: Describes a solution with the same solute concentration (osmolarity) as the cell, so there is no net movement of water
A pump protein that uses one ATP to move three Na⁺ ions out of the cell and two K⁺ ions into it
The model of membrane structure in which proteins are embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer and can move laterally
The movement of particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP and specific pump proteins
items.answer: The model of membrane structure in which proteins are embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer and can move laterally
items.markingKey: C. "fluid mosaic model" is the model of membrane structure in which proteins are embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer and can move laterally.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A channel protein in the membrane that allows rapid passage of water molecules"?
items.answer: aquaporin
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of aquaporin.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "active transport".
items.answer: The movement of particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP and specific pump proteins
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the movement of particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP and specific pump proteins. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how the fatty acid composition of membranes affects their fluidity.
items.answer: Unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bonds causing kinks; they cannot pack closely, so the membrane is more fluid; saturated fatty acids are straight, pack tightly and make membranes more viscous; organisms adjust composition to temperature.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bonds causing kinks; they cannot pack closely, so the membrane is more fluid; saturated fatty acids are straight, pack tightly and make membranes more viscous; organisms adjust composition to temperature. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The phospholipid tails face the water on both sides of the membrane." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The hydrophobic tails face inward towards each other; the hydrophilic heads face the water.
items.markingKey: The hydrophobic tails face inward towards each other; the hydrophilic heads face the water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does facilitated diffusion show a maximum rate at high concentration gradients?
options: All the carrier or channel proteins become occupied.
items.answer: All the carrier or channel proteins become occupied.
items.markingKey: D. Limited number of transport proteins.

items.stem: Which distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using ATP.
items.answer: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using ATP.
items.markingKey: C. Both use specific proteins; only active transport needs energy.

items.stem: "Gated channels pump ions using ATP." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Gated channels allow passive facilitated diffusion when open; they do not use ATP. Pumps use ATP.
items.markingKey: Gated channels allow passive facilitated diffusion when open; they do not use ATP. Pumps use ATP. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the fluid mosaic model and the Davson–Danielli model.
items.answer: Davson–Danielli proposed a static bilayer sandwiched between continuous protein layers; the fluid mosaic model has proteins embedded in or attached to a fluid bilayer, able to move laterally.
items.markingKey: Davson–Danielli proposed a static bilayer sandwiched between continuous protein layers; the fluid mosaic model has proteins embedded in or attached to a fluid bilayer, able to move laterally. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "In osmosis, water moves from low water concentration to high water concentration." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Water moves from a region of lower solute concentration (higher water potential) to higher solute concentration (lower water potential).
items.markingKey: Water moves from a region of lower solute concentration (higher water potential) to higher solute concentration (lower water potential). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe phagocytosis of bacteria by neutrophils and explain what it reveals about endocytosis.
items.answer: Neutrophils extend the membrane around bacteria and enclose them in a vesicle that fuses with lysosomes. Membrane fluidity allows the engulfing of large particles, which are then digested.
items.markingKey: Context (Neutrophils extend the membrane around bacteria and enclose them in a vesicle that fuses with lysosomes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Membrane fluidity allows the engulfing of large particles, which are then digested. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to endocytosis.

Briefly describe the Frye–Edidin cell fusion experiment (1970) and explain what it reveals about the fluidity of membranes.
items.answer: Mouse and human cells with differently labelled membrane proteins were fused; within 40 minutes the labels were intermixed. Proteins diffuse laterally in the bilayer, supporting the fluid nature of the model.
items.markingKey: Context (Mouse and human cells with differently labelled membrane proteins were fused; within 40 minutes the labels were intermixed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A beetroot cylinder had a mass of 1.99 g before and 2.28 g after 30 minutes in a sucrose solution. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: +14.6 %; mass gain = water entered by osmosis (solution hypotonic); mass loss = water left (hypertonic).
items.markingKey: % change = (2.28 − 1.99)/1.99 × 100 (M1) = +14.6 % (A1). Explanation (R1): mass gain = water entered by osmosis (solution hypotonic); mass loss = water left (hypertonic).

items.stem: Root hair cells take up nitrate ions even when the soil concentration is lower than inside the cells. Uptake stops when oxygen is removed. What does this show?
options: Nitrate is taken up by active transport, which needs ATP from aerobic respiration.
items.answer: Nitrate is taken up by active transport, which needs ATP from aerobic respiration.
items.markingKey: B. Uptake against a gradient dependent on respiration.

items.stem: With reference to Antarctic icefish living at −1.9 °C, explain how it illustrates adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity.
items.answer: Their membranes contain a high proportion of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Kinked unsaturated chains prevent membranes becoming rigid at freezing temperatures.
items.markingKey: Context (Their membranes contain a high proportion of polyunsaturated fatty acids.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Kinked unsaturated chains prevent membranes becoming rigid at freezing temperatures. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to adaptations that maintain membrane fluidity.

Cylinders of sweet potato were weighed, placed in sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 24 hours at 25 °C, blotted and reweighed.

Sucrose / mol dm⁻³ | Initial mass / g | Final mass / g | % change in mass
0.0 | 2.21 | 2.61 | +18.1
0.1 | 2.25 | 2.54 | +12.9
0.2 | 1.85 | 1.97 | +6.5
0.3 | 2.18 | 2.20 | +0.9
0.4 | 2.00 | 1.91 | ?
0.5 | 2.14 | 1.91 | -10.7

(a) Calculate the percentage change in mass in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. [2]

(c) Estimate the sucrose concentration that is isotonic with the tissue. [2]
items.answer: (a) -4.5 % (b) The cylinders had different initial masses; percentage change allows fair comparison. (c) ≈ 0.32 mol dm⁻³
